1037.title: Always there
1037.hook: women's stories were often unrecorded, but they were always there
1037.howItsDone: Jewish communities and schools increasingly teach women's history alongside the familiar story, reading the women of the Bible closely and gathering the letters, memoirs and Yiddish prayers that women left behind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, antisemitism today, and your line: hate returns, courage too. Today a new stretch begins, with the people the record kept leaving out.

Open the book of Exodus to its first chapter. A king of Egypt orders that every Hebrew baby boy be killed at birth. The text never gives that king's name. He is just Pharaoh. But two women stand between his order and the babies, and the text names them both: Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives. The man with the throne goes unnamed; two women who deliver babies get their names written down. For long stretches of the history we've been walking through, it ran the other way.
screen: `A KING WITH NO NAME.` → `TWO MIDWIVES, NAMED.` → `THE RECORD OFTEN RAN THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." A quiet refusal in a birthing room, by women with no army. Later books name more women: Miriam with her timbrel at the sea, Deborah judging Israel under a palm tree, Ruth on the road, Esther in the palace. Then come the long centuries after the Bible. Much of what was written down in them was written by men, about what men argued over in the study house and the court. A great deal of women's lives went unrecorded. Who lit the candles each Friday in a cold room. Who ran the shop while her husband studied. Who kept the recipes, songs and accounts, and taught a child the first blessing. But the record leaves traces: in the margins of old books, in letters, in the memoir a merchant woman named Glikl wrote in Yiddish for her children, in Yiddish prayers written for women to say over the candles and the dough. Historians have spent a long time gathering them. So today's line isn't a complaint or a slogan. It's a correction to how we read. When a page of history seems to be all men, it often means the women were in the next room, keeping the whole thing alive, and nobody was taking notes. Over the next days you'll meet some of them by name: a seamstress who started a school, a rabbi, a girl at a lectern, a writer, a teacher. They were always there.
screen: `THE MIDWIVES SAID NO.` · `NAMED IN THE BIBLE.` · `UNRECORDED FOR CENTURIES.` · `TRACES IN LETTERS AND PRAYERS.` · then, large: `ALWAYS THERE.`

segments.voice: Call up a woman from your own family line, or someone else's: a grandmother, a great-aunt, a neighbor who raised half the street. What do you actually know: her name, where she lived, one thing she made or said or kept? Notice where your knowledge stops, the edge where her story went unrecorded, and rest with her there, just as she was.
Always there. The women of Jewish history, from the midwives of Exodus to the grandmothers no one wrote about, present the whole time, even where the record left them out. Today's word.
Your line: nobody was taking notes. The women were there all along. See you tomorrow.

1038.title: Sarah Schenirer
1038.hook: a Kraków seamstress who founded the Bais Yaakov girls' schools in 1917
1038.howItsDone: Bais Yaakov schools today teach girls Torah, prayer, Jewish law and history, largely within Orthodox and Haredi communities, and they trace their story back to Sarah Schenirer's first class in Kraków.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women who were always there, and your line: nobody was taking notes. Today one of them steps out with a name.

A sewing room in Kraków, in Poland. Fabric on the table, pins in a cushion, a woman measuring a customer for a dress. Her name is Sarah Schenirer, and she is a seamstress. As she works, she listens. The girls and young women who come to her for clothes talk about novels, theater, new ideas from the wider world. Some of them, she notices, know very little of their own tradition. Their brothers spend their days learning Torah; the girls have nowhere to go for it. In 1917, with no money, no title and no school building, she does something about it.
screen: `A SEWING ROOM IN KRAKÓW.` → `GIRLS WITH NOWHERE TO LEARN.` → `SHE OPENS A SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: She began with a small class of girls in her own rooms, and called the school Bais Yaakov, the house of Jacob. The name comes from a verse. At Mount Sinai, just before the Ten Commandments, God tells Moses: "Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel." Why say it twice? An old rabbinic reading answers: the house of Jacob means the women, and the children of Israel the men. In that reading, the women were addressed first, and she made it her school's name. This was not a protest against her community. She was a devout woman in a traditional world, and she went looking for the support of respected rabbis, and found it. Her argument was simple. Girls would be the mothers and teachers of the next generation, in a world full of every other idea, so they needed to know their own texts, prayers and history, seriously. So she taught them. Then she trained young women as teachers and sent them out to start more schools. Her one room grew into a movement of schools across Poland and beyond. Bais Yaakov schools still exist today in many cities, teaching what she wanted taught: that girls belong in Jewish learning. A seamstress makes a garment one measurement, one cut, one seam at a time. She built a school system the same way.

1039.title: Regina Jonas
1039.hook: the first woman ordained a rabbi, in 1935, murdered at Auschwitz
1039.howItsDone: Women rabbis and Jewish communities remember Regina Jonas in study, sermons and memorial events, and her papers are read today as part of the history of women in Jewish leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarah Schenirer, and your line: a seamstress starts a school. Today, a woman in Berlin who wanted to stand where only men had stood. Go gently; this story ends in the camps.

A student in Berlin sits down to write a thesis. She is studying at a college that trains rabbis, and her question is one the people around her argue about: can a woman hold the office of rabbi? She answers not with a feeling but with sources: the Bible, the Talmud, the codes of Jewish law, page after page. Her conclusion is yes. Her name is Regina Jonas. The college lets her finish her studies, and then will not ordain her. So what does she do with a yes that nobody will sign?
screen: `A THESIS IN BERLIN.` → `CAN A WOMAN BE A RABBI?` → `A YES NOBODY WILL SIGN.`

segments.voice: She keeps going. In 1935, a rabbi named Max Dienemann examined her privately and signed her rabbinic ordination. She is remembered as the first woman known to have been ordained a rabbi. Germany was already under the Nazis, and Jewish life was being squeezed, rule by rule. Congregations were losing their rabbis, who fled or were pushed out, and Regina Jonas went where she was needed: she preached, taught, visited the sick and the old, and comforted people who were losing everything. Then she was deported to Theresienstadt, the ghetto and camp in the occupied Czech lands. Even there she kept working as a rabbi. She lectured, and helped meet the frightened people coming off the trains. From there she was sent to Auschwitz, and murdered. And then she was forgotten. For a long time her papers lay in an archive in Berlin, and her name dropped out of the story. When they were found, the women who had become rabbis since learned that someone had gone before them. In her own writing she argued, in effect, that God gives gifts and a calling to the heart without asking whether it belongs to a man or a woman. So today's line is two words: the first. Not a trophy, but a weight. Being first meant arguing alone, serving in the worst of times, and then being lost. Remembering her is part of the work.
screen: `ORDAINED, PRIVATELY, IN 1935.` · `A RABBI WHERE RABBIS HAD FLED.` · `SHE KEPT TEACHING IN THERESIENSTADT.` · `FORGOTTEN, THEN FOUND.` · then, large: `THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Who in your life did a thing before anyone like them had: the first in your family to finish school, the first woman in a job, the first to say something true out loud? Think of what it cost them to go first, and what it made easier for whoever came after. If you pray, you can remember Regina Jonas in your own words; if not, simply say her name once, quietly.

1040.title: The first bat mitzvah (1922)
1040.hook: Judith Kaplan becomes a bat mitzvah in New York
1040.howItsDone: In Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative synagogues a bat mitzvah girl may read from the Torah scroll and lead prayers; in Orthodox communities that mark it, the milestone is marked with a talk on a text she has studied, a women's gathering or a family celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Regina Jonas, and two heavy words: the first. Today, a much smaller first, on a Shabbat morning in New York.

A Shabbat morning in a synagogue in New York, in 1922. The Torah has been read, as it is every week. Then a girl named Judith Kaplan walks up to the front. Her father is the rabbi, Mordecai Kaplan, and he has decided that what boys do at this age, his daughter will do too. She says the blessings. She reads a passage of Torah aloud, in Hebrew and then in English, from a printed book. Then she sits down. No party plan, no theme, no DJ. And with it, the bat mitzvah as many Jews now know it began to take shape.
screen: `A SHABBAT MORNING IN NEW YORK.` → `A GIRL WALKS TO THE FRONT.` → `SHE SAYS THE BLESSINGS.`

segments.voice: Bar mitzvah, for a boy, and bat mitzvah, for a girl, mean son and daughter of the commandment. In Jewish law, a child grows into the age of the commandments: from then on, the mitzvot are theirs to keep, not just their parents' to teach. That happens to a girl whether there's a ceremony or not. Judith Kaplan's Shabbat added a public moment to mark it, in front of the community. And the first one was careful. She didn't read from the scroll itself, but from a printed book, after the regular reading, standing a little apart. Even so, people noticed. Her father wanted Judaism to change with the lives Jews actually lived, and a girl standing up in the synagogue was part of that; he later founded the movement called Reconstructionist Judaism. Then the idea spread, slowly at first, through different movements, each in its own way. Today in Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative synagogues, a girl may read from the Torah scroll itself, just as a boy does. In Orthodox communities that mark it, it happens in other ways: a girl gives a talk on a passage she has studied, celebrates with women and family, or takes on a project of learning or kindness. The Torah itself imagines everyone gathered to hear it: "Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn." A girl at a lectern is one way of answering that verse.

1041.title: Women rabbis
1041.hook: Reform ordains a woman in 1972, Reconstructionist in 1974, Conservative in 1985; Orthodox communities debate women's roles
1041.howItsDone: Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative seminaries ordain women as rabbis and cantors; in Orthodox communities some institutions train women for teaching and advisory roles under new titles, while other Orthodox authorities hold that the rabbinate is for men.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bat mitzvah, and your line: a girl at a lectern. Today, the question that girl's generation left for the next ones.

Five sisters walk up to Moses, in front of the priest, the leaders and the whole congregation: Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad. Their father has died with no sons, and with no son to inherit, his name and his share of the land will be lost to the family. They ask: why should our father's name be done away? Give us a possession. Moses doesn't answer on his own. He brings their case before God, and the answer comes back: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right." A new law of inheritance follows. Women standing up in front of everyone, asking the tradition a question.
screen: `FIVE SISTERS BEFORE MOSES.` → `THEY ASK A QUESTION OF THE LAW.` → `THEY SPEAK RIGHT.`

segments.voice: At the end of the same chapter, Moses hands leadership to Joshua. "And he laid his hands upon him, and gave him a charge." That laying on of hands is called semikhah, the word Jews still use for rabbinic ordination. For a long time, only men received it. Then the movements of modern Judaism each faced the sisters' kind of question, in their own time and their own way. Reform Judaism ordained a woman rabbi in 1972, the Reconstructionist movement in 1974, and the Conservative movement, after a long debate over Jewish law, in 1985. Each decision came with arguments from the sources, and people on more than one side. In Orthodox communities the question is still open, and argued with real seriousness. Some Orthodox institutions now train women in Jewish law and give them roles with new titles: teaching, answering questions, serving congregations. Other Orthodox authorities hold that the rabbinate belongs to men, and that women's leadership should take other forms. Both sides argue from the same Talmud, the same codes, the same respect for the law. So this isn't a story with a finish line. It's how Jewish law moves: someone asks, the community argues, sometimes the answer changes and sometimes it doesn't, and the question stays open to the next person who asks. The debates continue.

1042.title: Women's Torah learning
1042.hook: advanced Torah learning for women flourishes across communities
1042.howItsDone: Women study Bible, Talmud and Jewish law in women's study halls (midrashot), yeshivot and programs across Jewish communities, from Orthodox to Reform, and women teachers lead classes and complete the Talmud in study circles; communities differ on what is studied and where it leads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women rabbis, and your line: the debates continue. Today, something communities on different sides of that debate have made room for.

A long table, late in the evening. Two women sit across from each other with a page of Talmud between them. One reads a line out loud. The other says, wait, that can't be right, look at the next line. They argue. They lean in. Someone at the next table shushes them, then joins in. This is a study hall, a beit midrash, and the noise is the point. For a long time, rooms like this were almost entirely men's. Today there are rooms like this full of women, in Jerusalem, New York, London and elsewhere. How did that happen?
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE PAGE OF TALMUD.` → `THE NOISE IS THE POINT.` → `A ROOM THAT WAS MEN'S.`

segments.voice: The argument is old. In the Mishnah, in a passage about the ordeal of a wife suspected of adultery, a sage named Ben Azzai says a father should teach his daughter Torah. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees, sharply. Both opinions were written down. For a long time the cautious view shaped what girls were taught: prayers, laws for the home, the Bible in their own language, but not the Talmud. Yet there were exceptions. The Talmud itself remembers a woman named Beruriah, whose learning the rabbis respected and quoted. And a verse in Proverbs gives today its phrase: "Hear, my son, the instruction of thy father, And forsake not the teaching of thy mother." In Hebrew, the teaching of thy mother is torat imecha. Your mother's Torah. In modern times, things began to move. After Sarah Schenirer's schools came places for adult women to learn the full range of texts: Bible, Talmud, Jewish law. In Israel these are often called midrashot; in America and elsewhere there are women's study programs and yeshivot of many kinds. Women now teach Talmud classes, write commentaries, and finish the whole Talmud together and celebrate it, the way men's study circles do. Communities draw the lines in different places: what is studied, who teaches whom, what the learning leads to. But across communities that disagree about a great deal else, women's serious study has a place. Learning grows.

1043.title: Grace Aguilar
1043.hook: a nineteenth-century English Jewish writer and teacher
1043.howItsDone: Grace Aguilar's books are read today in Jewish women's history and literature courses, and her retellings of biblical women are studied as an early example of Jewish women interpreting scripture for one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two women over one page of Talmud, torat imecha, and your line: learning grows. Today the week ends with a writer.

A young woman in England sits at a desk, a Bible open and a pen in her hand. She is Jewish, from a family whose ancestors, the family remembered, had once hidden their Judaism in Portugal to survive. Around her, English Jewish girls are growing up reading English books, and some of the books about the Bible they can read in their own language were written by people hoping to persuade them to leave Judaism. She has a simple thought: our women should hear the Bible's women from one of their own. Her name is Grace Aguilar, and she picks up the pen.
screen: `A DESK IN ENGLAND.` → `A FAMILY THAT ONCE HID.` → `SHE PICKS UP THE PEN.`

segments.voice: Grace Aguilar lived in the nineteenth century and wrote in English, for English-speaking Jews: novels, poems and books of religious teaching. In The Spirit of Judaism she wrote about faith as something felt and lived in the heart and the home, not only kept by rule. In The Women of Israel she went through the Bible woman by woman, Sarah, Rebekah, Miriam, Deborah, Ruth, Hannah and on, telling their stories for Jewish women readers. Part of her point was an answer. Some writers of her day claimed that Judaism held women low. She went back to the text and said, in effect: look at these women, and how the Torah speaks of them. A verse from the last chapter of Proverbs fits the whole project: "She openeth her mouth with wisdom; And the law of kindness is on her tongue." She also wrote a novel, The Vale of Cedars, about Jews in Spain who had to hide their faith, the history her own family carried. And she taught: with her mother she kept a small school for boys at home. Her health was poor, and she died young, while traveling in Germany. Her books kept being read after her. Now look back at the week: the women who were always there, a seamstress who started a school, a rabbi in Berlin, a girl at a lectern, the debates that continue, learning that grows, and today a writer. Each one made her own place inside the tradition, and wanted it heard.
